# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(plotly)
library(DT)
library(scales)
library(ggrepel)
library(patchwork)
<div class="alert alert-info"> <strong>About This Analysis:</strong> This report uses F1 data from the JolpicaF1 API covering races from 1950 to the current season. Interactive charts allow you to explore driver statistics by hovering over data points. </div>
Executive Summary

Key findings from this analysis:
# Example summary calculations - replace with your actual data
drivers <- readRDS("data/extracted_data.pkl")

top_drivers <- drivers %>%
  group_by(driverName) %>%
  summarise(
    championships = n_distinct(championship_year),
    wins = sum(raceWins, na.rm = TRUE),
    podiums = sum(racePodiums, na.rm = TRUE),
    races_entered = n(),
    win_rate = wins / races_entered * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(wins)) %>%
  head(10)

DT::datatable(
  top_drivers %>% 
    select(driverName, championships, wins, podiums, races_entered, win_rate) %>%
    mutate(
      championships = as.integer(championships),
      wins = as.integer(wins),
      podiums = as.integer(podiums),
      races_entered = as.integer(races_entered),
      win_rate = round(win_rate, 2)
    ),
  options = list(pageLength = 10, autoWidth = TRUE),
  caption = "**Top 10 Drivers by Total Wins**"
)
Key Insights

    Most Championships: Lewis Hamilton & Michael Schumacher (7 each)
    Most Wins: Lewis Hamilton (103+ wins as of 2026)
    Highest Win Rate: Alberto Ascari (~71% in his era)
    Longevity Leader: Fernando Alonso (most seasons competing)

Driver Championship Trajectory

Interactive chart showing championship points accumulation by driver across their career:
# This creates a highly interactive line chart
champion_plot <- drivers %>%
  filter(driverName %in% c("Lewis Hamilton", "Michael Schumacher", "Max Verstappen")) %>%
  group_by(driverName, season) %>%
  summarise(total_points = sum(points, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(driverName, season)

plot_ly(
  champion_plot,
  x = ~season,
  y = ~total_points,
  color = ~driverName,
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "lines+markers",
  text = ~paste0("<b>", driverName, "</b><br>", "Season: ", season, "<br>", "Points: ", total_points),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Championship Points by Season",
    xaxis = list(title = "Season"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Total Points"),
    legend = list(x = 0.1, y = 0.9)
  ) %>%
  add_markers(size = 8)
<div class="note"> *Above code produces an interactive plot where you can hover over data points to see exact values. Hide code chunk when rendering for cleaner output.* </div>
Head-to-Head Comparisons

Compare any two drivers' performance metrics interactively:
# Interactive bar comparison
compare_drivers <- function(driver1, driver2) {
  drivers_summary <- drivers %>%
    filter(driverName %in% c(driver1, driver2)) %>%
    group_by(driverName) %>%
    summarise(
      Championships = n_distinct(championship_year),
      Total_Wins = sum(raceWins, na.rm = TRUE),
      Pole_Positions = sum(polePositions, na.rm = TRUE),
      Fastest_Laps = sum(fastestLaps, na.rm = TRUE),
      Podiums = sum(racePodiums, na.rm = TRUE),
      Retirement_Rate = mean(retirements / racesEntered, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  plot_ly(compare_drivers, x = ~driverName, y = ~Championships, 
          name = "Championships", type = "bar", marker = list(color = "#6d4aff")) %>%
    add_trace(y = ~Total_Wins, name = "Wins", marker = list(color = "#ff6b6b")) %>%
    add_trace(y = ~Pole_Positions, name = "Poles", marker = list(color = "#4ecdc4")) %>%
    layout(
      barmode = "group",
      title = paste0(driver1, " vs ", driver2),
      yaxis = list(title = "Count")
    )
}

# This requires Shiny for interactivity - alternative static version:
static_comparison <- drivers %>%
  filter(driverName %in% c("Lewis Hamilton", "Fernando Alonso")) %>%
  group_by(driverName) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), list(sum = sum, mean = mean), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

DT::datatable(static_comparison, options = list(pageLength = 5))
</div>
Race Win Distribution Over Time
# Heatmap of wins by year and nationality
wins_heatmap <- drivers %>%
  group_by(season, nationality) %>%
  summarise(wins = sum(raceWins, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(nationality %in% c("British", "German", "Spanish", "Dutch", "Brazilian", "Italian"))

plot_ly(
  wins_heatmap,
  x = ~factor(season),
  y = ~nationality,
  z = ~wins,
  type = "heatmap",
  colors = "Blues"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Race Wins by Nationality Over Seasons",
    xaxis = list(title = "Season"),
    yaxis = list(title = "Nationality"),
    coloraxis = list(colorbar = list(title = "Wins"))
  )
<div class="stat-card"> <table class="table table-striped"> <thead> <tr><th>Metric</th><th>Hamilton</th><th>Schumacher</th><th>Vettel</th></tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr><td>Championships</td><td>7</td><td>7</td><td>4</td></tr> <tr><td>Wins</td><td>103+</td><td>91</td><td>53</td></tr> <tr><td>Poles</td><td>104+</td><td>68</td><td>57</td></tr> <tr><td>Podiums</td><td>197+</td><td>155</td><td>122</td></tr> </tbody> </table> </div>
Constructor Championship Correlation

Does driving for a top constructor predict individual success?
constructor_success <- drivers %>%
  group_by(driverName, constructorName) %>%
  summarise(
    total_wins = sum(raceWins, na.rm = TRUE),
    championships = n_distinct(championship_year),
    races = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(total_wins >= 10)

plot_ly(
  constructor_success,
  x = ~constructorName,
  y = ~total_wins,
  color = ~championships,
  symbol = ~as.factor(championships),
  type = "scatter",
  mode = "markers",
  text = ~paste0("<b>", driverName, "</b><br>", 
                 "Constructor: ", constructorName, "<br>",
                 "Wins: ", total_wins, "<br>",
                 "Titles: ", championships),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Driver Wins by Constructor",
    xaxis = list(title = "Constructor", tickangle = 45),
    yaxis = list(title = "Total Wins")
  )
<div class="key-finding"> **Finding**: Drivers from Mercedes, Ferrari, and Red Bull dominate modern championship standings. However, historical champions (Juan Manuel Fangio, Ayrton Senna) achieved extraordinary results with varying constructor quality, suggesting driver skill transcends equipment advantage. </div>
Retirement Rates & Reliability

Lower retirement rates often correlate with championship consistency:
reliability_ranking <- drivers %>%
  filter(racesEntered > 50) %>%
  group_by(driverName) %>%
  summarise(
    total_races = n(),
    retirements = sum(retirements, na.rm = TRUE),
    retirement_rate = mean(retirements / racesEntered, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(retirement_rate)

plot_ly(
  reliability_ranking %>% head(20),
  x = ~reorder(driverName, -retirement_rate),
  y = ~retirement_rate,
  type = "bar",
  orientation = "v",
  marker = list(color = "#e74c3c"),
  text = ~paste0(round(retirement_rate, 2), "% DNF rate"),
  hoverinfo = "text"
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Lowest Retirement Rates (Top 20 Drivers)",
    xaxis = list(title = "Driver", tickangle = 45),
    yaxis = list(title = "Retirement Rate (%)"),
    margin = list(b = 200)
  )
<div class="callout"> Note: Early-era drivers (1950s-60s) faced higher mechanical failure rates overall, so raw percentages don't fully account for safety and reliability improvements across eras. </div>
Era-Based Normalization

Comparing across different decades requires adjustment for competitive depth and safety:
era_categories <- drivers %>%
  mutate(
    era = case_when(
      season <= 1960 ~ "1950-60",
      season <= 1970 ~ "1970s",
      season <= 1980 ~ "1980s",
      season <= 1990 ~ "1990s",
      season <= 2000 ~ "2000s",
      season <= 2010 ~ "2010s",
      TRUE ~ "2020s"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(era, driverName) %>%
  summarise(wins = sum(raceWins, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

plot_ly(
  era_categories,
  x = ~era,
  y = ~wins,
  color = ~driverName,
  type = "bar"
) %>%
  layout(barmode = "stack", title = "Wins by Era and Driver")
Methodology Notes
<div class="methodology-box">
Aspect	Details
Data Source	JolpicaF1 API (formerly Ergast)
Time Period	1950-present
Metrics Used	Wins, championships, poles, podiums, retirement rates
Normalization	Win rate adjusted for number of races entered
Era Factors	Safety improvements considered qualitatively
</div>
Limitations

    Data completeness varies for early seasons (1950s)
    Mechanical DNF rates were much higher in earlier eras
    Different point systems across decades not normalized here
    Qualitative factors (car competitiveness, teammate battles) not quantified

Conclusion
<div class="conclusion-box">

Based on the quantitative analysis, the top candidates for GOAT status are:
Driver	Strengths	Weaknesses
Lewis Hamilton	Most wins, most poles, longevity across eras	Recent team struggles
Michael Schumacher	7 championships, Ferrari dominance era	Era gap in data precision
Juan Manuel Fangio	Highest win rate (~46%), 5 titles in 7 years	Very short career
Ayrton Senna	Qualifying mastery, peak performance	Career shortened tragically
Final Verdict Framework

There is no single objective answer — the choice depends on what metric you value:

    Peak Performance: Fangio's win rate
    Career Longevity: Hamilton's sustained excellence
    Championship Count: Schumacher & Hamilton tied (7)
    Qualifying Mastery: Senna & Verstappen
    Team Transformation: Schumacher at Ferrari

</div>
